sections.title: Ports & Protocols You Must Memorize
sections.content:
Port numbers identify the Layer-4 service. Memorize these cold — the exam tests them directly.
Port | Protocol | Transport | Purpose
20/21 | FTP | TCP | File transfer (20 data, 21 control)
22 | SSH / SCP / SFTP | TCP | Secure remote shell & file transfer
23 | Telnet | TCP | Remote CLI — insecure, cleartext
25 | SMTP | TCP | Sending email between servers
53 | DNS | TCP & UDP | Name resolution (UDP queries, TCP zone transfers)
67/68 | DHCP | UDP | Automatic IP configuration (67 server, 68 client)
69 | TFTP | UDP | Trivial file transfer (no auth) — firmware, PXE
80 | HTTP | TCP | Web, cleartext
110 | POP3 | TCP | Retrieve email (download)
123 | NTP | UDP | Time synchronization
143 | IMAP | TCP | Retrieve email (sync across devices)
161/162 | SNMP | UDP | Monitor/manage devices (162 = traps)
389 | LDAP | TCP/UDP | Directory services
443 | HTTPS | TCP | Web over TLS
445 | SMB | TCP | Windows file/printer sharing
514 | Syslog | UDP | Log messages to a collector
636 | LDAPS | TCP | Secure LDAP
993 | IMAPS | TCP | Secure IMAP
995 | POP3S | TCP | Secure POP3
3389 | RDP | TCP | Remote Desktop (Windows GUI)
exam_tips: Secure pairs: HTTP 80 -> HTTPS 443, FTP 21 -> SFTP 22, LDAP 389 -> LDAPS 636, Telnet 23 -> SSH 22.
DNS uses UDP 53 for lookups but TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses.
SNMP get/set is UDP 161; SNMP traps (device-initiated alerts) are UDP 162.

sections.title: TCP vs UDP
sections.content:
Both are Layer-4 transport protocols; the choice is reliability vs speed.
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — connection-oriented, reliable. Uses the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to set up a session, sequences and acknowledges segments, retransmits loss, and controls flow. Used by web, email, file transfer, RDP.
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) — connectionless, best-effort. No handshake, no acknowledgements, no retransmit. Lower overhead and latency. Used by DNS, DHCP, NTP, SNMP, VoIP, streaming, and online games where speed beats perfect delivery.
Three-way handshake: Host A -> SYN -> Host B; Host B -> SYN/ACK -> Host A; Host A -> ACK -> Host B. Teardown uses FIN/ACK exchanges.
exam_tips: Reliable, ordered, acknowledged = TCP. Fast, lightweight, real-time = UDP.
Memorize the handshake order: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

sections.title: Traffic Types & Protocol Concepts
sections.content:
Traffic delivery types:
Unicast — one sender to one specific receiver (most traffic).
Broadcast — one sender to every host on the subnet (e.g., ARP requests). IPv4 only; stops at the router.
Multicast — one sender to a group of interested receivers (e.g., streaming, routing updates). Uses 224.0.0.0/4.
Anycast — one sender to the nearest of several hosts sharing one address (common for DNS root servers, CDNs).
IPv6 note: IPv6 has no broadcast — it uses multicast and anycast instead.
Other key protocols: ICMP (ping, traceroute, error messages — Layer 3), ARP (resolves IP to MAC on the local link), GRE and IPsec (tunneling/VPN), and IP itself (connectionless Layer-3 delivery).
exam_tips: IPv6 replaces broadcast entirely with multicast/anycast.
ARP maps IP -> MAC on the local segment; it is a Layer 2/3 helper, not routable.

concept_cards.hook: TCP's connection setup: SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK. Establishes sequence numbers before data flows.
One-to-one delivery to a single specific destination address — the bulk of network traffic.
One-to-many delivery to a group of subscribed receivers, using the 224.0.0.0/4 range in IPv4.
One address shared by many hosts; traffic is routed to the nearest one. Used by DNS root servers and CDNs.
An unsolicited alert a managed device sends to the SNMP manager (UDP 162) when an event occurs, instead of waiting to be polled.
Trivial File Transfer Protocol (UDP 69) — a lightweight, no-authentication file transfer used for firmware, configs, and PXE boot.
Address Resolution Protocol — resolves a known IPv4 address to its MAC address on the local link so frames can be delivered.
A standard for sending event/log messages to a central collector, typically over UDP 514.

practice_questions.q: Which port does the secure version of LDAP (LDAPS) use?
practice_questions.explanation: LDAP is TCP/UDP 389; LDAPS (over TLS) uses TCP 636.

practice_questions.q: SNMP traps are sent to the manager on which port?
practice_questions.explanation: SNMP polling uses UDP 161; device-initiated traps use UDP 162.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol and port transfer files securely over an SSH session?
practice_questions.explanation: SFTP runs over SSH on TCP 22; FTPS (separate) uses 990.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol retrieves email and keeps it synchronized across multiple devices?
practice_questions.explanation: IMAP syncs mail across devices; POP3 typically downloads and removes it.

practice_questions.q: Windows file and printer sharing uses which protocol and port?
practice_questions.explanation: SMB (Server Message Block) uses TCP 445 for Windows file/printer sharing.

practice_questions.q: A broadcast frame is sent to which type of audience?
options: Every host on the local subnet
practice_questions.explanation: Broadcast reaches all hosts on the subnet; it does not cross a router.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol provides connectionless, best-effort delivery with no handshake?
practice_questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless and best-effort — no handshake, acknowledgements, or retransmission.

practice_questions.q: Which statement about IPv6 traffic types is correct?
options: IPv6 adds a new broadcast range
IPv6 uses multicast and anycast but has no broadcast
practice_questions.explanation: IPv6 replaces broadcast with multicast and anycast.

practice_questions.q: Which port and transport does HTTPS use?
practice_questions.explanation: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) uses TCP port 443.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol and port provide secure remote shell access?
practice_questions.explanation: SSH uses TCP 22 and encrypts the session; Telnet (23) is cleartext.
